lesson.grammar_point: sequencing and argument markers for a structured case (to begin with, secondly, furthermore, what is more, consequently, it follows that, finally, to sum up)

listenings.text: I coach people who have to speak in public, and almost all of them have the same problem. They know exactly what they want to say, but the audience doesn't know where they are. So the first thing I teach is signposting. To begin with, tell people how many points you have. Three is perfect. Five is too many, and nobody remembers seven. Secondly, when you move to a new point, say so out loud: 'My second point is about cost.' It sounds obvious, but it works like a sign on a highway. Without it, people get lost, and when people get lost, they stop listening. What is more, never apologize for your structure. When a speaker says, 'Sorry, this part is a bit boring,' the room switches off immediately. Finally, end with one sentence that people can repeat at dinner that night. If you do these things, your audience will remember the path, and not just the last joke. A good talk isn't a list of facts. It's a walk, and you are the guide.

I've sat as an arbitrator in more than sixty cases, and I can usually tell in the first five minutes of an opening statement whether counsel is well prepared. The good ones give us a map. To begin with, they tell us what the dispute is about in two sentences. Then they tell us what they are going to prove, and in what order. Furthermore, they keep their promises. If they say there are three issues, I hear three issues, not seven. The weak ones read thirty pages of their written submission out loud. Consequently, by the second hour, half the tribunal is looking out of the window. It follows that the best openings are often the shortest ones. My advice to young lawyers is simple. First of all, assume that we have read the file, because we have. Secondly, tell us what you want us to decide, and why. Finally, stop when you have finished. In thirty years, nobody on a tribunal has ever complained that an opening statement was too short.
